The United Kingdom is no longer within the EU legislative system. Parliament, domestic regulators and UK courts determine its cryptoasset order, subject to retained or assimilated law and international obligations. The result is staged: existing financial-services categories, anti-money-laundering registration and financial-promotion rules operate now, while a wider statutory regime has been enacted for later commencement.1

UK firms may still encounter EU law by serving EU clients or establishing within a Member State. Equivalence, recognition or cooperation cannot be presumed. A UK permission does not constitute a MiCA authorisation, and an EU authorisation does not itself satisfy UK requirements. The two orders influence each other commercially but remain legally distinct.

English courts treated cryptoassets as property capable of supporting proprietary relief before Parliament intervened. AA v Persons Unknown accepted Bitcoin as property for an interim proprietary injunction.2 The Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025 now confirms that a thing is not prevented from being an object of personal property rights merely because it is neither a thing in possession nor a thing in action.3 The Act removes a categorical barrier; it does not declare every digital record property or settle every incident of ownership.

Courts have adapted freezing, proprietary and information remedies to pseudonymous transactions. Relief still depends on jurisdiction, a serious issue, evidence linking assets or defendants, and procedural fairness. Orders against exchanges can be effective because an identifiable intermediary holds records or controls withdrawals. They do not establish a general judicial power over every network participant.

Some token arrangements fall within the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 because they embody specified investments or because an activity is regulated. Others sit outside that traditional perimeter. Classification therefore turns on rights and activity, not marketing terminology. The 2026 Cryptoassets Regulations establish the legal basis for a broader regime, but the Financial Conduct Authority states that the new regime will begin on 25 October 2027.4

At the cut-off, cryptoasset businesses within scope must comply with Money Laundering Regulations registration, and promotions to UK consumers must comply with the financial-promotion regime even where the promoter is overseas.5 Registration is not a general prudential licence or endorsement. Firms should not describe the future 2027 regime as presently operative.

Stable-value arrangements may engage payment-services, electronic-money, banking or future cryptoasset rules depending on structure. The policy choice is not simply whether a token is “stable”; it is who owes redemption, what backs the claim, where reserves sit and what happens on failure. The comprehensive regime's later start makes transition and public communication especially important.

The UK's Digital Securities Sandbox permits controlled modification of specified legislative requirements for eligible market-infrastructure activity. A sandbox is a bounded statutory environment, not a waiver of all law. Tokenisation can alter issuance and settlement processes while leaving the underlying security, issuer duties, market-abuse controls and finality questions intact.

Property recognition is only the first step in failure. A customer must establish the nature of the entitlement, the governing terms, segregation or trust arrangements, and any shortfall allocation. Wallet labels and on-chain balances do not by themselves prove the intermediary's liabilities. Custody rules should therefore join legal characterisation to operational reconciliation and return procedures.

The Law Commission's 2023 final report recommended targeted development rather than a closed statutory taxonomy.6 The 2025 Act implements the core recognition point while leaving courts to develop incidents case by case. That approach preserves common-law adaptability but requires litigation capacity and cannot replace clear sectoral rules for licensed custodians.

MiCA is an EU regulation and is directly applicable within Member States according to its terms.7 It allocates functions among national competent authorities, the European Banking Authority and the European Securities and Markets Authority. This legal form differs fundamentally from voluntary regional coordination.

Member States designate authorities, exercise options and apply sanctions and procedure within the EU framework. National contract, property, insolvency, company and procedural law continues to matter where EU law does not fully harmonise the consequence. A MiCA authorisation therefore does not answer every ownership or insolvency question.

MiCA creates disclosure and conduct rules for offers and admission to trading, and authorisation and organisational duties for cryptoasset service providers. It also creates a passport within the Union under specified conditions. The passport is possible because a supranational regulation and common institutional architecture supply the legal basis; it is not a generic benefit of licensing.

MiCA distinguishes asset-referenced tokens from electronic-money tokens and imposes issuer, reserve, redemption, governance and supervisory requirements. Significance can trigger enhanced oversight. The categories show the value of separating the reference mechanism, issuer obligation and use in payment from market vocabulary.

Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 extends originator and beneficiary information requirements to transfers of cryptoassets involving covered providers.8 Compliance requires verified data, handling of missing information and risk-based decisions. It does not make every unhosted-wallet transfer unlawful; the applicable duties depend on regulated-provider involvement and the Regulation's conditions.

MiCA authorisation does not displace anti-money-laundering law. Customer due diligence, suspicious-transaction reporting, sanctions screening and record retention operate through the EU and Member-State AML architecture. Information sharing must retain legal purpose, confidentiality and redress.

Regulation (EU) 2022/858 permits authorised DLT market infrastructures to operate within a supervised pilot subject to limits and possible exemptions.9 The pilot is evidence-generating legislation: it allows specified departures while preserving entry, reporting, investor-protection and exit controls.

DLT financial instruments remain financial instruments. Settlement assets, finality, delivery-versus-payment and access to central-bank money remain institutional questions. A ledger cannot confer settlement finality unless the governing law gives the recorded event that consequence.

Capital, own-funds, safeguarding and insurance requirements respond to different loss channels. Outsourced custody can concentrate technology and legal risk even where each firm meets an individual requirement. Supervision should examine group structure, common service providers and the recoverability of customer records.

The Digital Operational Resilience Act applies a harmonised framework for ICT risk, incident reporting, resilience testing and critical third-party oversight to covered financial entities.10 Its contribution is organisational, not merely technical: boards retain responsibility when functions are outsourced.

The General Data Protection Regulation requires a lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, security and observance of transfer rules.11 Immutability does not excuse unlawful processing. System design should distinguish public transaction data from identity, compliance and supervisory records and avoid placing unnecessary personal data on a public ledger.

Digital identity can reduce duplicate verification and improve inclusion, but creates concentration and exclusion risks. Supervisory access must be authorised, necessary and logged; private firms should not receive undefined public powers. Privacy and financial integrity require structured access rather than a choice between anonymity and total visibility.

The UK combines common-law recognition with staged financial legislation. The EU combines a directly applicable market code with residual national private law. Neither model eliminates classification, institutional capacity or transition. Their different constitutional bases explain why an EU passport and UK judicial development cannot be copied as isolated devices.

Pakistan can adapt express issuer redemption duties, activity permissions, custody safeguards, operational-resilience governance, proportionate promotions rules and versioned transition. It should not assume EU-style supranational institutions, nor leave core customer-asset consequences wholly to litigation. Domestic constitutional competence and the notified PVARA baseline remain controlling.

The two orders reveal a common sequence beneath their different legal forms. A regulator first identifies the activity and responsible person; entry requirements then test governance, capital and systems; continuing rules govern conduct, custody and reporting; failure rules protect customers and preserve records; and courts or review bodies determine contested applications. Pakistan's Regulations address significant parts of entry and continuing conduct. Primary and institutional work remains necessary at the interfaces, especially property, insolvency, tax, banking and constitutional review.

Stablecoin regulation illustrates the sequence. MiCA legislates distinct issuer categories and supervisory consequences. The UK is moving toward a domestic regime through staged legislation and rules. Neither model permits the label “stablecoin” to answer reserve ownership, redemption, payment use or failure. Pakistan should require the responsible issuer to state the holder's enforceable claim, reserve assets and custodian, valuation, reconciliation, redemption time, suspension events and insolvency consequence before public distribution.

Custody supplies a second test. Property recognition under the 2025 UK Act makes it possible for a digital object to support personal property rights, but the Act does not prove that a particular platform holds the object for the customer. MiCA's custody and organisational rules improve regulated conduct but leave residual national private law. Pakistan therefore needs both: a technology-neutral recognition rule and prescriptive duties making customer entitlement reconstructable across omnibus wallets and sub-custody chains.

The comparison also warns against confusing regulatory scale with legal simplicity. MiCA's passport reduces repeated authorisation inside the Union because Member States share a regulation, institutions and judicial order. It also generates extensive technical standards and supervisory coordination. The UK's staged regime avoids claiming that future comprehensive rules already operate. Pakistan should use its single national framework to reduce duplication, but a licence should still list permitted activities and conditions rather than function as an unlimited badge.

Operational resilience should be owned at board level. DORA's most transferable insight is that outsourcing changes the delivery of a function, not the regulated firm's responsibility for it. A Pakistani provider using a cloud host, wallet technology vendor, analytics service or foreign custodian should map concentration, access, incident notification, termination and recovery. PVARA needs lawful access to sufficient evidence, while customer and personal data remain protected by purpose and security controls.

Data law creates a genuine tension with public ledgers. A firm cannot always delete or correct a public transaction record, yet it can avoid adding identity data, keep personal information off-chain, use revocable credentials and correct linked institutional records. Supervisory design should ask what information is necessary for licensing, AML, tax and redress and who may see it. An indiscriminate data lake would not be justified by either GDPR comparison or innovation policy.

Finally, both orders show the value of transition candour. The FCA publicly distinguishes current registration and promotion duties from the regime commencing in October 2027. EU instruments specify application dates and transitional arrangements. Pakistan's institutions should do the same for each form, permission and continuing service. A clear date and a bounded continuity rule protect lawful reliance more effectively than informal assurance.

Enforcement architecture completes the comparison. UK regulators act within domestic statutory powers and their decisions are subject to domestic review; EU implementation combines national competent authorities with EBA, ESMA and the Court of Justice structure. Administrative cooperation does not eliminate the affected firm's right to know the case and challenge a decision. Pakistan should specify which body investigates, which imposes an administrative measure, what material may be withheld, when interim action is available and which forum reviews the result.

Market-abuse and promotion rules also need to be separated. A misleading advertisement may be actionable even where the asset itself falls outside a securities category; manipulation rules depend on the market and instrument within scope. MiCA supplies express conduct rules for covered cryptoassets, while the UK applies its promotions regime broadly to communications to UK consumers. Pakistan should give PVARA clear authority over regulated-service promotions and coordinate with SECP where a tokenised security is involved, avoiding double punishment for the same conduct.

The independent contribution of the comparison is thus institutional rather than ideological. Common-law adaptability and supranational codification can both protect markets if source, competence and remedies are visible. Each can also fail when customers cannot establish entitlement or regulators cannot supervise outsourced infrastructure. Pakistan's design should be judged by those operational questions rather than whether its statute resembles London or Brussels.

That judgment should be published periodically. A concise implementation report can state permissions granted, processing time, customer-asset exceptions, material incidents, complaints, appeals and supervisory limitations. Comparable evidence would allow legislators to decide whether primary law, Regulations or institutional resources need adjustment, and would keep formal legal convergence from concealing weak execution.

Pakistan should also preserve a public perimeter archive. As in the UK's staged change and the EU's application of successive instruments, a transaction must be tested against the law then in force. The archive should show effective dates, transitional permissions, superseded guidance and the status of each provider. This protects both enforcement and legitimate reliance and prevents later policy from being projected backwards.

The UK and EU demonstrate two credible routes toward a digital-asset order, but neither is a single template. Public authorisation, private rights, AML controls, resilience and data law must meet at operational interfaces. Pakistan's task is to allocate those interfaces expressly and to state when a new permission becomes legally and practically available.

This chapter stands as a comparative account of UK and EU law at the cut-off. UK readers should note the scheduled 25 October 2027 commencement of the comprehensive regime; later rules or commencement changes require updating.

Japan and South Korea regulate exchanges within detailed national frameworks; Singapore and Hong Kong use financial-centre institutions; China restricts private virtual-currency business while developing state digital money; India combines tax and AML obligations with unresolved perimeter questions; Australia is transitioning to new platform licensing; New Zealand relies substantially on existing law. These differences follow constitutional authority, capital controls, monetary policy and market history.

Licensing, prohibition, sandbox experimentation and central-bank digital currency are different legal techniques. A state may permit wholesale tokenisation while restricting retail promotion; it may tax a transaction without licensing the service; and it may develop a CBDC without recognising private tokens as money. Comparison must keep those propositions separate.

The Mt Gox failure made custody, insolvency and record integrity central to Japanese policy. Early judicial reasoning did not treat Bitcoin as a corporeal thing capable of ownership under the particular Civil Code inquiry, but this did not place exchange claims outside law. Claims, restitution and insolvency distributions continued through contractual and statutory structures. The episode warns against deriving an entire regulatory perimeter from one property-law characterisation.

The Payment Services Act requires registration for cryptoasset exchange services and imposes information, security, segregation and supervisory duties. Stablecoin reforms distinguish electronic payment instruments and limit issuance or intermediation through designated regulated actors. Japan also applies FATF-style transfer-information duties; an August 2026 amendment expanded covered jurisdictions.1 Precise commencement and counterparty scope remain essential.

Singapore regulates digital payment token services through the Payment Services Act 2019, Monetary Authority of Singapore notices and amendments extending the perimeter to specified cross-border and custody activities. A licence is activity-specific. AML, technology risk, safeguarding and conduct requirements may differ by service and customer class.2

Singapore's Electronic Transactions Act supports automated contracting subject to ordinary requirements of attribution and validity. Project Guardian and related institutional pilots explore tokenised funds and wholesale markets. A pilot or industry standard is not general permission: regulated issuance, dealing, custody and settlement continue to depend on applicable legislation and MAS authority.

Centralised virtual-asset trading platforms operating in Hong Kong are subject to the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance licensing regime; platforms dealing in security tokens may also require authorisation under the Securities and Futures Ordinance. The Securities and Futures Commission applies a dual-licensing approach and detailed platform guidelines.3

Hong Kong combines licensed retail platform access with institutional tokenisation and a distinct fiat-referenced stablecoin regime. The Stablecoins Ordinance commenced on 1 August 2025, and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced its first licences in April 2026.4 Licensing an issuer does not settle the treatment of every tokenised security, platform or custody arrangement.

The 2021 multi-agency notice treats virtual-currency-related business activities as illegal financial activities and addresses overseas exchanges serving domestic residents.5 This is a restrictions model, not merely an unlicensed-market model. Any account must preserve the distinction between private holding, prohibited business services and enforcement practice rather than state that “crypto is banned” without qualification.

China's support for blockchain applications and its digital-renminbi programme coexist with restrictions on privately issued and traded virtual currencies. The apparent tension disappears once the state distinguishes infrastructure from private monetary substitution. For Pakistan, the lesson is that technology policy, payment sovereignty and private-asset regulation are separable decisions.

The Act on the Protection of Virtual Asset Users took effect on 19 July 2024. It imposes customer-deposit and custody safeguards, requires a high proportion of customer virtual assets to be kept in cold wallets, and addresses unfair trading and supervisory enforcement.6 The statute is a protection layer; it does not by itself settle every issuer or business category.

South Korea continues to develop its second-stage market architecture. August 2026 amendments strengthened registration and AML controls for virtual-asset service providers, with provisions commencing according to the official instrument.7 Tax commencement has been politically contested; comparative claims should cite the current tax statute and effective date rather than repeated announcements.

In Internet and Mobile Association of India v Reserve Bank of India, the Supreme Court set aside the RBI's 2018 banking circular on proportionality grounds.8 The judgment did not declare virtual assets legal tender, create a licence, or prevent Parliament and regulators from acting within lawful authority. It is principally a case about evidential justification and the proportionality of a particular restriction.

India taxes income from transfers of virtual digital assets under section 115BBH and requires covered providers to comply with anti-money-laundering registration and guidance.9 Tax and AML coverage do not amount to comprehensive market authorisation. Private-law characterisation, service permissions and the treatment of decentralised arrangements remain questions requiring the relevant statute and facts.

ASIC applies existing corporations, financial-products, consumer and market law according to the rights and activities involved. Some cryptoassets are financial products; others are not. Misleading conduct and managed-investment-scheme rules can apply without a special token label.10

The Corporations Amendment (Digital Assets Framework) Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 8 April 2026 and introduces a licensing framework for covered digital-asset platforms and tokenised custody platforms. ASIC states that the new requirements commence on 9 April 2027 and has set an implementation path.11 Until commencement, present law continues; passage should not be described as present operational authorisation.

In Ruscoe v Cryptopia Ltd (in liquidation), the High Court held that cryptocurrencies were property under the Companies Act 1993 and that the exchange held specified assets on trust for account holders.12 The holding depended on New Zealand law and the platform arrangements. It is persuasive comparative authority, not a universal declaration of customer priority.

New Zealand applies financial-markets, fair-trading, AML and financial-service-provider law according to activity. The Financial Markets Authority has warned that particular offers or services may be regulated even without a bespoke cryptoasset code. Cryptopia shows why regulatory coverage should be joined to clear custody records and insolvency rules.

Across the region, the durable elements are express entry controls, segregation and reconciliation, market-conduct prohibitions, operational resilience and lawful transition. Property recognition and market authorisation answer different questions. Pakistan's notified PVARA Regulations provide a current licensing baseline; implementation should state how existing providers enter it and how customer assets are treated during transition and failure.

Financial-centre models rely on regulators, courts, payment systems and professional capacity that took time to build. Restriction models reflect different monetary and political choices. Pakistan should adapt mechanisms only after identifying the domestic institution, statute, resources and route of review that will make them real.

The first regional lesson concerns institutional memory after failure. Mt Gox and Cryptopia made the legal status of customer assets and the quality of platform records unavoidable. South Korea translated loss experience into statutory deposit and cold-wallet protections; Japan imposed segregation and exchange supervision. The transferable rule is not a fixed cold-storage percentage. It is the requirement that a supervisor and insolvency office-holder can reconstruct each customer's entitlement, identify control, detect a shortfall and activate a lawful return or distribution process.

The second lesson is that payment policy can diverge from investment-market policy. China supports distributed technology and a state digital currency while restricting private virtual-currency business. Indonesia permits supervised cryptoasset trading while maintaining a separate payment perimeter. Hong Kong regulates trading platforms and stablecoin issuers through different statutes and institutions. Pakistan should therefore resist using PVARA licensing to imply that an asset is legal tender, an authorised payment instrument or freely convertible under foreign-exchange law.

The third lesson is staged statutory commencement. Australia enacted a new framework in April 2026 but set commencement for April 2027. That interval allows rules, applications and systems to be prepared while existing law continues. Hong Kong's stablecoin law tied issuer entry to a commenced statutory regime and official licensing. Pakistan's regulations are already the current baseline; its next transition task is different. It must publish how an incumbent completes the application, which existing services may continue, what marketing is prohibited and what occurs on refusal.

The fourth lesson is that constitutional adjudication can improve regulatory method without deciding substantive policy. The Indian Supreme Court's proportionality ruling addressed the evidential foundation and breadth of a banking restriction. It did not confer monetary or licensing status. Pakistani regulators should similarly assemble evidence, identify affected rights, compare less restrictive means and give reasons, particularly where account access, blocking or compulsory exit is proposed.

The fifth lesson is to distinguish institutional experiments from general law. Singapore's wholesale tokenisation projects can test issuance, settlement and interoperability in a sophisticated market. They do not prove that retail distribution, custody or cross-border offers are generally permitted. A Pakistani sandbox should specify participants, modified or applicable rules, customer limits, data access, test metrics, exit and the legal effect of results. Graduation should require an ordinary permission or legislative change.

These comparisons also counsel against rankings. A restrictive jurisdiction may have a clear monetary policy but limited private innovation; a permissive financial centre may impose demanding entry and customer controls; a country taxing gains may still lack a complete service-provider regime. “Adoption” and “friendliness” are poor legal metrics. The questions that matter are whether citizens can know the law, firms can obtain a definite decision, assets survive failure, misconduct is investigated and restrictions can be challenged.

For Pakistan, institutional fit should be evidenced through capacity before scale. PVARA needs licence examiners, custody and technology specialists, a supervisory dataset and an exercised incident process. SBP and SECP need a recorded interface for mixed products. FBR needs valuation and reporting rules. Courts and investigators need admissible records. Comparative legislation becomes useful only when these domestic connections are made.

The licensing record should show more than an entity name. Japan, Hong Kong and South Korea demonstrate the importance of linking a provider to its activities and continuing duties. Pakistan's public register should list exchange, brokerage, custody, transfer, lending, issuance or other permissions separately, identify conditions and show suspension, surrender or wind-down. A customer should be able to distinguish a preliminary incorporation approval from a final activity licence without reading a press release.

Regional experience also supports risk-based foreign recognition rather than automatic equivalence. A provider licensed in Singapore, Hong Kong or Australia may be well supervised, but Pakistani authorities still need access to records, cooperation, customer remedies and a lawful route when permission changes abroad. Recognition should specify the activity and can be withdrawn on stated grounds. It should never imply that foreign monetary, tax or insolvency law displaces Pakistan's mandatory rules.

Finally, comparison should remain dynamic but source-controlled. Asia-Pacific regimes changed rapidly between 2024 and 2026. An annual review should record enactment, commencement, official rule changes, licensing evidence and leading judgments in separate columns. Policy speeches and consultation papers can explain direction but should not overwrite the current-law column. This discipline is particularly important where reform dates have been deferred or a pilot is described as a national framework.

Market integrity requires the same functional method. South Korea's unfair-trading controls, Hong Kong's platform supervision and Japan's exchange rules operate within distinct statutes. Pakistan should define manipulation, deceptive conduct, conflicts and misuse of customer orders for the markets it actually supervises. Surveillance data should support investigation, not automatically determine liability. Where SECP securities law and PVARA rules both engage the same conduct, referral and penalty coordination should preserve lawful competence and prevent duplicate punishment.

Retail access should be evaluated through evidence rather than foreign fashion. Suitability, warnings, leverage restrictions and product limits can reduce harm, but excessive complexity or broad banking exclusion can shift citizens to offshore channels. Pakistan should monitor complaints, losses, access, concentration and unauthorised-provider use, and revise controls through published reasons. That balanced feedback loop is more transferable than any region's present list of permitted assets.

Courts remain part of that loop. IAMAI and Cryptopia answered different constitutional and private-law questions, yet both show the value of reasoned adjudication when regulation or failure exposes an unresolved assumption. Pakistan should ensure that PVARA decisions generate a record fit for review and that insolvency proceedings can obtain custody evidence. Comparative doctrine is most useful when it improves that domestic decisional method.

Asia-Pacific comparison defeats simple categories. Permission may coexist with strict retail controls; state tokenisation may coexist with restrictions on private currencies; and tax or AML coverage may coexist with an incomplete market perimeter. The correct comparative question is not which jurisdiction is friendliest, but which institution performs each legal function and with what evidence of operational capacity.

[21.01] This chapter examines the GCC setting, the United Arab Emirates’ federal order, Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority, the ADGM and DIFC financial free zones, and the approaches of Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman and Kuwait. It also considers Islamic-finance governance and cross-border capital. Each permission is analysed by territory, issuer, activity and regulator. The chapter rejects the assumption that one licence supplies access across a federation or region.

[21.02] The Gulf Cooperation Council supports coordination, integration and connection between Member States, including in economic and financial affairs.1 It has not, however, created a directly applicable digital-asset code comparable to the European Union’s MiCA regime. Licensing, monetary policy, securities law and enforcement remain national or, where lawfully established, free-zone functions. Regional similarity should not be converted into a fictional passport.

[21.03] Member States compete for capital through different regulators, free zones, tax settings and innovation programmes. Competition can accelerate rulemaking and expertise, but it can also produce overlapping claims. Comparative analysis must identify the territory, excluded zones, regulated activity and legal status of every instrument.

[21.04] Federal Cabinet Decisions Nos 111 and 112 of 2022 established a framework for virtual assets and their service providers outside financial free zones and delegated specified federal competencies to Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority.2 The framework interacts with emirate-level and free-zone laws. A provider must therefore map where it operates and which activity it performs rather than rely on a generic ‘UAE licence’.

[21.05] The Central Bank of the UAE regulates payment-token services within its monetary and banking remit. Its Payment Token Services Regulation defines the territorial and activity scope, prohibits unlicensed payment-token services and establishes licence categories.3 Federal Decree-Law No 32 of 2025 established the Capital Market Authority as the legal successor to the Securities and Commodities Authority; references in legislation to the former authority are now read accordingly.4 Token form does not displace the underlying regulator’s competence.

[21.06] Dubai Law No 4 of 2022 created the Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority. VARA’s territorial remit covers Dubai, including development and free zones, but excludes the Dubai International Financial Centre.5 The exclusion is constitutionally and commercially important: the DIFC has its own regulator and courts.

[21.07] VARA combines compulsory company-wide rulebooks with activity-specific modules for advisory, broker-dealer, custody, exchange, lending and borrowing, management and investment, transfer and settlement, and issuance.6 This makes obligations traceable to functions. Its value nevertheless depends on supervision, inspections, enforcement and orderly exit, not the modular presentation alone.

[21.08] The Abu Dhabi Global Market and Dubai International Financial Centre are distinct financial free-zone legal orders with their own regulators and courts under UAE constitutional and federal arrangements. ADGM’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority has developed and updated a virtual-asset framework; the Dubai Financial Services Authority regulates crypto-token financial services in the DIFC under rules updated with effect from 12 January 2026.7

[21.09] Common-law courts and specialised regulators can improve commercial predictability, but only within their jurisdiction. A free-zone entity may still encounter onshore marketing, payment, employment, insolvency or enforcement rules. Interfaces need formal memoranda, referral rules and judicial conflict methods; a corporate address cannot settle them.

[21.10] The Central Bank of Bahrain requires a licence for regulated cryptoasset services and specifies the relevant service categories and licence classes.8 Centralising monetary and market-supervision functions can reduce institutional ambiguity, but also demands sufficient specialist capacity and transparent due process.

[21.11] Bahrain’s framework combines governance and conduct controls with segregation, cyber-security, anti-money-laundering and reporting obligations. Its 2025 stablecoin module requires a licence and, for the covered single-currency stablecoins, full reserve backing and redemption controls.9 A stablecoin permission answers only the specified issuance and service activities; it does not immunise securities, payments or consumer conduct.

[21.12] In 2018 the Saudi Standing Committee warned that virtual currencies were not official currencies and that no parties were then licensed to trade them in the Kingdom.10 That dated warning should not be converted into a timeless general prohibition. The current legal question remains activity-specific: banking, payment, securities and promotional conduct each require authority under the competent regime.

[21.13] The Saudi Central Bank’s regulatory sandbox and the Capital Market Authority’s Financial Technology Experimental Permit provide controlled routes for testing eligible innovations.11 These routes separate experimentation from market-wide authorisation. Pakistan can adopt bounded testing only if entry, affected rules, customer exposure, data access and exit consequences are published and legally controlled.

[21.14] The Qatar Financial Centre introduced a Digital Assets Framework in 2024 for permitted tokens and token-service activities within the QFC. Its rules expressly exclude tokens used as currency substitutes or means of payment, including cryptocurrencies and stablecoins, from the permitted-token category.12 The framework is therefore a controlled tokenisation regime, not a general cryptoasset permission.

[21.15] Oman’s Financial Services Authority has issued instructions for registering virtual-asset service providers and applying anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing requirements, while continuing work on a broader framework.13 Kuwait’s Capital Markets Authority Circular No 10 of 2023 prohibits specified uses, investments, licensing and mining activities within its stated remit and links contravention to the penalties in the Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism Law.14

[21.16] These approaches cannot be collapsed into a regional average. Registration for financial integrity is not a market licence; a financial-centre framework is not necessarily nationwide permission; and a prohibition must be read for scope, authority and exceptions. The disciplined comparator is the legal effect of each instrument.

[21.17] There is no single universally controlling Shariah characterisation of every digital asset. Analysis may differ by asset, jurisdiction, institutional board and contractual structure. A lawful product-governance process should identify the asset and promises, obtain reasoned Shariah review where represented as compliant, manage conflicts and monitor continuing conformity. The Islamic Financial Services Board’s 2025 principles emphasise the institutional allocation of responsibility, procedures, conflicts controls, review and audit rather than a universal product label.15

[21.18] Asset backing does not by itself establish compliance, and volatility does not by itself decide it. Product design should examine riba, excessive gharar, maysir, sale of what is not owned, custody, redemption, risk allocation and connection to the real economy. Claims of compliance must be specific, documented and institutionally accountable.

[21.19] Free zones can concentrate courts, regulators, professional services and international capital. Their effectiveness comes from a complete institutional package, not reduced friction alone. Market access outside the zone, banking connectivity and recognition of judgments remain separate questions.

[21.20] Firms may allocate issuance, custody, management and marketing across different entities. Supervisors therefore need group maps, beneficial ownership, consolidated risk information and lawful exchange arrangements. Cooperation should preserve confidentiality and contestability; it should not create powers that domestic law has not conferred.

[21.21] Modular rulebooks, precise activity permissions, public registers, specialist supervision and defined interfaces are transferable techniques. Pakistan’s final Virtual Asset Services Regulations and Activity Specific Regulations were notified on 21 August 2026 under SROs 1419(I)/2026 and 1420(I)/2026.16 Speed is valuable only when valid instruments are supported by staff, systems, supervision and courts.

[21.22] The general regulations state their hierarchy, territorial reach and proportional licensing approach. They also require PVARA to maintain a public register of licensed providers.17 That register should identify the legal entity, regulator, activity, customer class, conditions, effective date and current status of each permission.

[21.23] Modularity allows a common governance base to be joined to activity risk. A custodian needs key control, segregation and recovery; an exchange needs order handling, surveillance and conflicts management; an issuer needs disclosure, reserves and redemption; and a transfer service needs execution and financial-integrity controls. Modules should be cumulative where one group performs several activities. Group structure should not permit interconnected functions to be distributed among affiliates to avoid combined-risk supervision.

[21.24] Pakistan cannot reproduce an emirate/free-zone architecture without constitutional authority. Regulatory design must respect federal and provincial legislative competence, equality and property protections, the constitutional allocation of judicial power and High Court review.18 Branding an enclave as innovative cannot cure an unlawful delegation.

[21.25] The Virtual Assets Act 2026 establishes a Virtual Assets Appellate Tribunal and provides a further appeal to the Supreme Court.19 A specialist tribunal can improve first-instance expertise only if appointments, procedure, independence, reasoned decisions and appeals are operational. Its statutory jurisdiction must coexist with, and cannot displace, the constitutional jurisdiction of the superior courts.

[21.26] The UAE comparison shows why geographic scope belongs on every public register. A provider may be licensed for a particular activity by VARA in Dubai outside the DIFC, by the DFSA in the DIFC, by the FSRA in ADGM or under a federal framework. Customers encountering a common national brand may not understand those distinctions.

[21.27] A Gulf licence may make a provider commercially credible but does not answer whether it may solicit Pakistani customers, hold their assets abroad or transfer their data. Pakistan’s Act and regulations address territorial and extraterritorial reach and regulatory cooperation; recognition should still be activity-specific and conditional on lawful cooperation, equivalent outcomes, access to records, complaint handling and orderly withdrawal.20 Automatic passporting would outsource public protection without a treaty or common legal order.
