[21.28] Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman and Kuwait demonstrate that regulatory development can be selective. A state may authorise controlled testing, permit tokenisation within a financial centre, require AML registration, or prohibit specified activities while studying broader policy. A limited rule can be legitimate if its scope and rationale are clear. The danger lies in allowing pilots, warnings or registrations to carry legal meanings they do not possess.

[21.29] Institutional speed should be measured from valid decision to operational evidence, not press release to announcement. Useful evidence includes processed applications, examination findings, tested incident contacts, successful customer-asset reconciliation and reasoned enforcement or appeal outcomes. Pakistan’s sequencing should make the dependency between law, staffing and market infrastructure explicit.

[21.30] Failure planning is a necessary comparator. A provider may custody assets through an affiliate or foreign sub-custodian and serve customers elsewhere. Its insolvency can engage several courts and regulators despite a specialised home regime. Pakistan’s final regulations require custody controls, proof of reserves and insolvency-related arrangements.21 Providers should also maintain a custody-chain map, governing-law disclosure, portable records and an exercised transfer or return plan.

[21.31] Public finance deserves equal care. PVARA’s Fund is a statutory, lapsable fund subject to the Public Finance Management Act 2019. Constitutional custody, appropriation and audit controls continue to apply.22 A projected licence market should not justify commitments before lawful revenue and appropriation exist. Independence is strengthened by transparent funding and accountability, not by placing funds beyond ordinary control.

[21.32] Shariah governance may support regional cooperation, but any mutual-recognition scheme would need competent approval, defined standards, conflicts controls and the ability to revisit a product after its structure changes. The safer immediate approach is disclosure of the reviewing body, reasoning basis and continuing status so investors understand precisely what has and has not been certified. The financial regulator remains responsible for solvency, custody, disclosure and market conduct.

[21.33] Technology procurement is another capacity test. A regulator or provider may purchase sophisticated market-surveillance, custody and compliance systems, but public authority remains with the regulator. Pakistan should specify data ownership, access, model limitations, security, continuity, audit and exit before outsourcing. A vendor’s risk score should lead to review, not become an unpublished rule for licensing, account closure or enforcement.

[21.34] Competition policy should examine vertical integration. A group that issues a token, operates an exchange, provides custody, lends against the asset and controls a settlement token can concentrate conflicts and failure risk even where each module is individually licensed. PVARA should map the group, impose proportionate separation or governance controls and coordinate with the Competition Commission of Pakistan where dominance, restrictive agreements, deceptive marketing or merger questions arise.23

[21.35] Regional capital competition should not displace domestic public outcomes. Attraction of firms, assets under custody and transaction volume can rise while consumer recourse, market concentration or illicit-finance risk worsens. Pakistan should evaluate access, integrity, resilience, tax compliance and rights alongside investment. A competitive regime is one that produces reliable lawful service, not the lowest entry threshold.

[21.36] The final lesson is transparency about limits. An authority should say where its territory ends, where another regulator decides and where no permission yet exists. That candour reduces disputes and false reliance. Pakistan’s public positioning should make legal scope, customer protection, review and failure preparedness as visible as innovation opportunities.

[21.37] The GCC demonstrates that regulatory competition can coexist with disciplined licensing and specialised courts, but also that territorial boundaries matter. Pakistan’s best lesson is to make every permission legible by actor, activity, territory and regulator, and to join Islamic-finance claims to reasoned product governance rather than general labels.

[21.38] This chapter is an independent jurisdictional map, not a licensing opinion. Firms must verify the current rulebook, geographic scope and activity permission with the relevant official register.

ASEAN works through treaties, declarations, sectoral bodies and Member-State implementation. It has not conferred EU-style legislative competence for a directly applicable cryptoasset code. Regional declarations can organise cooperation and political commitment, but market permissions and sanctions depend on national law.

Member States differ in financial-market depth, capital controls, monetary priorities, legal systems and supervisory capacity. Divergence therefore appears in token classification, licensing, custody, payment use and enforcement. An accurate regional account identifies the national instrument and authority behind each proposition.

The 2023 ASEAN Leaders' Declaration supports regional payment connectivity, local-currency transactions and interoperable cross-border systems while taking country circumstances into account.1 This agenda concerns regulated payment rails and central-bank cooperation; it is not a regional permission for privately issued digital assets.

Payment links require common messaging, identity assurance, cyber resilience, foreign-exchange handling, dispute allocation and lawful data transfer. Cooperation should specify purpose, security and confidentiality. Interoperability without liability rules can transmit operational failure as efficiently as value.

Singapore supplies regional financial infrastructure, licensed digital-payment-token services and wholesale tokenisation initiatives. Its influence derives from MAS capacity, courts, banking connections and professional services. Pilot participation or incorporation in Singapore does not confer authority elsewhere.

Chapter 20 explains the Payment Services Act, provider licensing and institutional tokenisation in detail. For regional purposes the key point is interface: Singapore-based providers must still satisfy each destination state's marketing, payments, securities, AML and data rules.

Malaysia's Capital Markets and Services (Prescription of Securities) (Digital Currency and Digital Token) Order 2019 brings specified digital currencies and tokens within the Securities Commission's framework. The Commission regulates digital-asset exchanges through its Guidelines on Recognized Markets and issuance and custody through its Guidelines on Digital Assets.2 Revised exchange guidelines effective 20 May 2026 strengthen governance, financial and safeguarding requirements.3

Malaysia joins securities supervision to a developed Islamic-capital-market architecture. The Commission's Shariah Advisory Council may assess particular digital assets for trading on regulated exchanges. That status is asset- and market-specific, not a universal religious determination. Custody and token offerings retain issuer, disclosure, segregation and AML duties.

Indonesia historically treated cryptoassets as commodities for trading supervision while Bank Indonesia restricted their use as payment. Law No 4 of 2023 on Financial Sector Development and Strengthening reallocated digital financial-asset supervision toward the Financial Services Authority, OJK. Commodity classification and payment status answer different questions.

OJK Regulation No 27 of 2024 established the digital-financial-asset trading framework following the supervisory transfer; Regulation No 23 of 2025 expanded and strengthened it, including digital-asset derivatives.4 The transition illustrates the need for transferred records, licences, staff, investigations and customer protections—not only a statutory change of regulator.

Thailand's Emergency Decree on Digital Asset Businesses BE 2561 (2018), as amended, regulates digital-asset exchanges, brokers, dealers, fund managers, advisers and token portals through Ministry of Finance licensing and SEC supervision.5 The official English version is an unofficial translation; the Thai text controls.

Thailand distinguishes investment and trading services from payment policy. The 2025 amendment strengthens reach over offshore operators serving persons in Thailand and supports transaction suspension in technology-enabled crime cases.6 Extraterritorial reach still requires a statutory connecting factor and practicable cooperation.

Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Circular No 1108 of 2021 replaced the earlier virtual-currency-exchange framework with guidelines for virtual-asset service providers, including licensing, governance, AML, consumer protection and technology requirements.7 Securities or investment arrangements may additionally engage the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Virtual-asset services intersect with remittance and inclusion in a large cross-border labour economy. Lower transfer cost must be tested against fraud, volatility, cash-out access and recourse. Enforcement alerts and application moratoria are administrative measures with their own scope; they should not be represented as permanent statutory prohibitions.

Vietnam moved from an incomplete framework to a controlled pilot for a cryptoasset market under Government Resolution No 05/2025/NQ-CP, effective 9 September 2025.8 A pilot is bounded by its resolution, eligible operators and supervisory conditions. It does not retrospectively regularise all market activity.

Private cryptoassets have not thereby become lawful means of payment; payment-instrument rules and State Bank authority remain distinct. The Government's 2026–2030 programme contemplates further legislative development.9 Pakistan should read Vietnam as an example of staged experimentation, not a completed national code.

Malaysia uses securities prescriptions; Indonesia separates trading from payment and transferred supervision; Thailand has a bespoke decree; the Philippines uses payment and AML supervision; Vietnam operates a pilot. All address digital assets, but their classifications, legal effects and enforcement bodies differ.

A regional table can conceal the decisive facts: whether the instrument is legislation or guidance, whether it has commenced, which activity is licensed and whether the provider may serve foreign customers. National law must remain visible in every comparison and cross-border contract.

QR linkages and fast-payment connections can reduce remittance cost without using a privately issued token. Their legal foundations include settlement finality, access criteria, foreign-exchange rules, scheme liability and central-bank cooperation. Technical connection is the last mile of a legal and institutional arrangement.

Private stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs allocate credit, redemption and governance differently. Regional initiatives should test which claim moves across the interface and which institution bears failure. “Interoperable” should never mean that these liabilities are legally identical.

Switzerland applies financial-market law and its DLT legislative amendments, including DLT trading facilities and ledger-based securities; FINMA supervises according to activity. Liechtenstein's Token and Trusted Technology Service Provider Act supplies a civil and supervisory framework. Canada applies provincial securities law and national AML rules, with platform registration coordinated through the Canadian Securities Administrators.10

El Salvador's legal-tender experiment, Brazil's virtual-asset legislation, South Africa's financial-product classification and offshore licensing centres illustrate different policy objectives. Small-state or offshore models may rely on foreign markets and external enforcement. Headline adoption should not be treated as evidence of inclusion, stability or institutional success.

Pakistan can pursue bilateral and regional payment links, AML cooperation, regulator-to-regulator assistance and common technical messaging without pretending that national laws are unified. Each arrangement should preserve domestic authority, data safeguards, liability and review.

The ASEAN experience favours staged entry, public registers, activity-specific duties and managed institutional transfer. Pakistan's present task is to operationalise its Act and notified Regulations, not imitate a foreign label. Any pilot must state its legal basis, limits, customer protections and exit path.

Regional payment connectivity provides a concrete model of cooperation without harmonised asset law. Central banks can link fast-payment systems, agree messages and foreign-exchange treatment, manage settlement and allocate operational responsibility while each state retains its currency and licensing rules. Pakistan can pursue comparable links through SBP and competent counterparts. A private stablecoin is not required for that objective, and should not be inserted into a public payment link without separate issuer, reserve and redemption authority.

Supervisory cooperation can follow the same pattern. A memorandum may establish contacts, consultation and information exchange, but each authority acts under its own law. Requests should identify purpose, permitted use, confidentiality and onward disclosure. Joint exercises can test cyber incidents, provider failure and customer transfer. Such practical cooperation is more credible than a declaration of common standards unsupported by compatible procedures.

The Indonesia transition is particularly relevant to Pakistan's institutional design. Moving supervision from a commodity authority to OJK required more than new legal text: licences, records, staff, investigations and market infrastructure had to move or be recognised. Pakistan's current challenge involves coordination rather than the same transfer, but the operational lesson holds. A provision assigning responsibility should be accompanied by data, personnel, procedure, budget and a tested handoff.

Malaysia illustrates how a capital-markets regulator can combine exchange, issuance and custody rules with Islamic-finance governance. Yet the Securities Commission acts under Malaysia's statutes and institutional history. Pakistan should not import a Malaysian Shariah classification as a market permission. It can require transparent product review, competence, conflicts management and ongoing monitoring while maintaining PVARA, SBP and SECP responsibility for the legal and financial consequences.

Thailand's 2025 extraterritorial amendment addresses offshore providers serving persons in Thailand. Pakistan likewise needs a connecting rule for remote providers. The rule should identify targeted marketing, local onboarding, payment channels, language, customer volume and other evidence of service into Pakistan. Worldwide website accessibility is too broad; voluntary evasion of a clear domestic customer connection is too narrow. Enforcement should combine local conditions with international cooperation and app or payment interventions authorised by law.

The Philippines and Vietnam show different uses of staged control. BSP's VASP framework builds on payment and remittance supervision, while Vietnam's pilot is a legally bounded experiment. Pakistan already has an Act and Regulations, so a nationwide pilot label would obscure the present baseline. It may still use sandboxes for a novel activity if the ordinary law identifies which requirements can be varied and how customers are protected.

The non-ASEAN comparators reinforce the point. Switzerland and Liechtenstein pair innovative statutory categories with established courts and financial supervision. Canada shows coordinated securities regulation without one national securities statute. Brazil, South Africa and other emerging markets adapt existing payment or financial-product law. An offshore centre may achieve fast incorporation but rely on foreign banks and enforcement. Pakistan should compare the complete institutional package and failure route, not the novelty of the statutory vocabulary.

This approach changes how “regional leadership” should be measured. The relevant indicators are cost and speed of lawful payments, clarity of market permissions, recoverability of customer assets, effectiveness of cooperation, cybersecurity and access to remedy. Volume of token trading or the number of memoranda does not establish those outcomes. Regional initiatives should publish evidence, limits and revision dates.

Pakistan's broader diplomatic position can then be coherent. It can support interoperable payments and tax or AML cooperation, recognise foreign permissions conditionally, and preserve domestic customer and monetary law. This is neither isolation nor false harmonisation. It is an architecture in which cross-border functions are connected while public authority remains traceable to the relevant state.

Regional data cooperation requires an additional safeguard. Identity and transaction information collected for a payment, AML or tax purpose should not be transferred for undefined innovation use. Agreements should identify the controller or custodian, accuracy process, security, retention, correction and breach response. Pakistan should establish these protections in domestic law before promising seamless supervisory data exchange.

Small and medium providers also matter. Capital and technology requirements can improve resilience while entrenching a few regional groups. Malaysia's 2026 strengthening of DAX governance and safeguarding illustrates the need to connect higher requirements to identified risks. Pakistan should assess proportionality, allow shared services under controlled outsourcing and monitor concentration, without lowering customer-asset or integrity standards.

An ASEAN-style model of incremental connectivity may therefore suit Pakistan better than an ambition for immediate comprehensive regional harmonisation. Begin with defined payment corridors, regulator contacts and evidence standards; test them; publish outcomes; then expand. Each new connection should identify the domestic rule it depends on and the event that would suspend it. Regionalism becomes credible when it is operationally narrow and legally complete.

Consumer redress must travel with connectivity. A user should know which provider received the instruction, when settlement became final, how foreign exchange was priced, who handles error and which forum hears the complaint. Regional payment links can allocate these questions through scheme rules and domestic law. Private-token arrangements need equivalent clarity about issuer, reserve, custodian and redemption. Lower cost without a recoverable claim is not durable inclusion.

Pakistan should also distinguish recognition from reliance. It may recognise that a foreign provider meets specified home-state outcomes and still require a local representative, disclosures, data access and customer-asset conditions. It may rely on a home supervisor for part of the examination while retaining the power to restrict local service. The decision should be written, activity-specific, reviewable and capable of withdrawal.

These controls make diversity an asset. ASEAN Member States can test different classifications and supervisory methods while sharing operational lessons. Pakistan can participate in regional learning without importing a whole regime or understating its own current law. Comparative material becomes a disciplined source of options, and domestic institutions remain responsible for the choice.

Future comparison should record whether initiatives produce accessible and recoverable services. A payment connection that works only for large banks, a licence that excludes smaller lawful firms without risk justification, or a pilot without a route to ordinary law may not advance inclusion. Pakistan should place distributional evidence beside technical performance and market volume when deciding whether to extend a regional arrangement.

ASEAN's achievement is practical cooperation amid legal diversity. Its payment-connectivity work shows that states can make systems interoperable while retaining monetary sovereignty. Its national frameworks show that transition and institutional allocation are substantive legal work. Pakistan can pursue both lessons without claiming a regional passport or completed harmonisation.
National instruments and official-language texts control; translations and regional declarations should be used according to their legal status.

This chapter maps the different legal effects of FATF, FSB, Basel Committee, CPMI, IOSCO, IMF, World Bank, OECD and UNIDROIT materials, together with accounting standards and supervisory cooperation. It explains how soft law can become operationally consequential without itself becoming Pakistani legislation. The chapter offers Pakistan a method for reasoned incorporation: identify the standard, domestic legal vehicle, competent institution, affected persons, evidence, safeguards and review.

Treaties, Security Council decisions, domestic statutes, regulations, institutional recommendations, technical principles and industry standards are not interchangeable. A treaty binds according to international law and domestic implementation; a regulator's rule binds through delegated authority; a standard may guide policy or assessment without directly creating an offence, tax or licence condition.

Soft law becomes consequential through legislation, licence conditions, supervisory expectations, correspondent relationships, market practice and external assessment. That influence can be intense while remaining legally mediated. Every domestic use should identify its enabling provision, scope, addressee and route of challenge.

Pakistan’s first question is methodological: what must be true before a foreign rule can support a domestic recommendation? Seven matters must be recorded. The comparison must identify: the Pakistani problem; the foreign instrument’s legal force; its institutional setting; the exact rule or outcome; Pakistan’s present baseline; the resulting delta; and the condition on which transfer would work. If one is missing, the comparison is descriptive rather than corrective.

This method distinguishes four kinds of material. A standard expresses an internationally agreed outcome but ordinarily requires domestic implementation. Guidance explains or supports implementation and must not be represented as binding text. A foreign enactment or rulebook binds within its own jurisdiction, not Pakistan. An implementation review reports what jurisdictions have done and may expose recurrent failure; it does not silently enlarge the underlying standard. Dates matter because a 2025 implementation review can qualify confidence in a 2023 framework without amending its text.

Comparators are selected by function, not prestige. FATF is used because Chapter 23 identified an enacted AML and Travel Rule foundation whose supervisory allocation and operating specification remain incomplete. FSB and IOSCO are used because Chapters 9, 10, 15 and 16 identified cross-regulator, multi-function, client-asset, market-abuse and enforcement questions. MiCA is used because Pakistan has enacted issuer and service-provider regimes but must complete their taxonomy and operating detail. CARF and DAC8 are used because Chapter 23 identified a tax-information problem distinct from licensing. VARA is used for instrument architecture. Hong Kong is used for platform terminology, token admission and custody controls. South Africa is used to test the narrower technique of adapting existing law. The question is never which jurisdiction is “best”; it is which design feature answers a proved Pakistani problem at acceptable legal and institutional cost.1

Three limits follow. First, similarity of words does not establish similarity of law. “VASP”, “CASP”, “VATP” and “licensed corporation” belong to different statutory settings. Secondly, a rule cannot be detached from the institution that administers it. EU passporting depends on the Union’s internal-market structure; Dubai’s rulebooks operate within VARA’s territorial mandate; Hong Kong’s platform regime connects to the SFC’s securities architecture. Thirdly, comparison does not decide constitutional competence, delegated authority, property character, tax liability or appellate jurisdiction in Pakistan. Those questions remain governed by Pakistani law.

FATF Recommendation 15 and its Interpretive Note require countries to assess virtual-asset risks and regulate or prohibit virtual-asset service providers consistently with the risk-based approach.2 The definitions are functional and designed for financial integrity. They do not determine private ownership, tax character or securities status.

FATF expects covered providers to obtain, hold and transmit specified originator and beneficiary information and to apply beneficial-ownership, targeted-financial-sanctions and proliferation-financing controls. Implementation must preserve data security, legal purpose and proportionality. The standard does not itself authorise indiscriminate surveillance or create a domestic offence.

Pakistan’s FATF question is: does the present order translate Recommendation 15 into an identifiable, supervised and testable system for every relevant VASP function, including offshore-facing and technology-mediated arrangements? The FATF Recommendations, as amended in June 2026, require countries to assess virtual-asset risk, license or register VASPs, apply preventive measures and effective supervision, and provide proportionate and dissuasive sanctions.3

Pakistan’s baseline is now statutory and regulatory. The Virtual Assets Act 2026 (Act XIII of 2026) deems licensed VASPs to be financial institutions for Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010 purposes, imposes specified AML/CFT/CPF duties on VASPs and issuers, and requires originator and beneficiary information for transfers at or above a threshold prescribed by PVARA. The Pakistan Virtual Asset Services Regulations 2026 were notified on 21 August 2026 as SRO 1419(I)/2026; regulation 100 fixes the Travel Rule threshold at the PKR equivalent of USD 1,000 and specifies core information and control requirements. The remaining delta is operational: supervisory allocation, goAML onboarding, secure messaging, aggregation and exception handling, counterparty controls, inspections, sanctions, appeals and evidence of effectiveness must work in practice.4

Pakistan’s second FATF question is: which actors fall within the functional perimeter when a business presents itself as software, DeFi or a protocol rather than a conventional company? FATF’s 2021 guidance and July 2026 DeFi report direct attention to activities actually performed and to whether a natural or legal person exercises control or sufficient influence. The domestic transfer condition remains a fact-and-control test under the enacted VASP definition. The regulatory file should identify persons who operate the business, retain administrative or upgrade power, control interfaces or fees, select counterparties, custody assets or exercise sufficient influence over performance. VASP status should not be inferred from publication of code, token ownership or participation alone.5

Pakistan’s third FATF question is: does enactment equal effectiveness? FATF’s seventh targeted update of 16 July 2026 reports further progress but continuing gaps in converting risk assessments into mitigation, operationalising licensing or registration, identifying actors and conducting effective risk-based supervision and enforcement. Its design lesson is not a league table; a legal rule is incomplete as a control until entities, supervisors, systems, tests, findings and remediation can be evidenced.6

For Pakistan, operational proof should include: a current public register tied to the confidential AML reporting population; entity-level goAML onboarding; a Travel Rule conformance suite; inspections of actual messages and exceptions; a process for foreign and unlicensed VASPs targeting Pakistan; documented risk treatment for self-hosted wallets; and aggregate effectiveness reporting. Notification of a regulation proves that an instrument was issued; it does not prove that the regulated population, supervisory systems or enforcement controls are functioning.

Pakistan should use FATF as the outcome baseline and maintain an authenticated AMLA–VAA–PVARA allocation showing who supervises each obligation, which data may move, how decisions are challenged and what evidence demonstrates effectiveness. The June and July 2026 FATF materials should be version-controlled rather than cited through an older implementation snapshot.

The FSB's 2023 global framework contains high-level recommendations for cryptoasset activities and global stablecoins, built around “same activity, same risk, same regulation”.7 It emphasises governance, data, risk management, cross-border cooperation and effective resolution. The formula requires functional analysis; it does not mean that unlike legal claims should receive identical rules.

FSB implementation reviews compare whether jurisdictions have converted recommendations into effective frameworks. Pakistan should use the comparison to identify gaps, publish its response to each recommendation and explain adoption, adaptation or rejection.

Pakistan’s FSB question is: can the regulatory perimeter follow economic function and financial-system connection when one group combines exchange, custody, lending, settlement, token issuance and proprietary activity? The FSB’s 2023 high-level recommendations are a global financial-stability baseline. They call for adequate powers and resources; comprehensive, functional and proportionate regulation; domestic and cross-border cooperation; governance; risk management; data and disclosure; monitoring of interconnections; and treatment of multi-function service providers. The FSB expressly limits its own mandate: the recommendations do not comprehensively cover AML/CFT, privacy, cybersecurity, consumer protection, market integrity, competition, tax, monetary policy or monetary sovereignty.8

Pakistan’s baseline includes an activity schedule, licensing powers, fit-and-proper review, customer and issuer duties, prudential delegation, data reporting and inter-agency provisions. The delta lies in the connections. PVARA’s licence cannot displace SBP’s payment, banking, currency or foreign-exchange functions, or SECP’s securities, company and futures jurisdiction. A combined group may create risks not visible in an activity-by-activity form: use of customer assets to support proprietary positions; common technology and wallet infrastructure; intra-group lending; correlated reserves; conflicts in token listing; and contagion through a shared treasury. Pakistan should require a consolidated function and dependency map, related-entity disclosure, common-risk assessment, restrictions or separation where conflicts cannot be managed, and shared supervisory products owned by the legally competent institutions.

Pakistan’s implementation question is: how much confidence should be placed in announced frameworks before supervisory performance is visible? The FSB’s 2025 thematic review found progress but significant gaps and inconsistencies, with less progress for global stablecoin arrangements and continuing cross-border difficulties. It assessed framework implementation as of August 2025, not the effectiveness of every regime. The lesson supports Chapter 23’s staged readiness test: published law, appointed institutions, valid instruments, connected data, trained supervisors, completed examinations, remediation and measured outcomes are separate states.9

Pakistan’s IOSCO question is: what market outcomes must a virtual-asset regime reproduce where activity is substitutable for securities-market intermediation? IOSCO’s 2023 final report contains eighteen recommendations organised around conflicts from vertical integration, market manipulation and fraud, custody and client assets, cross-border cooperation, operational and technological risk, and retail distribution. It seeks regulatory outcomes consistent with those applied in traditional financial markets, while allowing jurisdictions to use their own legal architecture.10

Pakistan’s baseline addresses fair dealing, conflicts, market manipulation, insider trading, custody, complaints, cyber controls and sanctions. The delta is specification and supervision. A platform should have documented token-admission criteria, surveillance ownership, proprietary-trading controls, order and price integrity rules, conflict disclosures, customer categorisation, custody reconciliations, incident escalation and a complaint-to-remedy path. Where a token or activity is already a security or futures product, the answer is not a parallel PVARA version of securities law. It is classification, referral or coordinated supervision under the competent statute.

Pakistan’s final IOSCO question is: does formal coverage show effective market supervision? IOSCO’s 2025 thematic review recorded meaningful implementation progress among participating jurisdictions but did not assess the effectiveness of application across authorisation, supervision and enforcement. Pakistan should therefore avoid claiming IOSCO alignment from legislative text alone. Alignment should be demonstrated through tested market surveillance, custody examinations, conflict remediation, enforcement reasons and cross-border cooperation outcomes.11

The Basel Committee's prudential standard classifies bank cryptoasset exposures into groups with differing capital treatment and imposes infrastructure, redemption and exposure conditions.12 It is addressed to bank supervision, not to the legality of public trading. Domestic effect comes through SBP's lawful adoption within Pakistan's banking framework.

BIS work distinguishes tokenised deposits, stablecoins and central-bank money by issuer liability, settlement asset and governance. Tokenising a deposit should not erase the bank's obligation or depositor protection. Cross-system arrangements must preserve finality and the singleness of money where that is the policy objective.

The Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures organise governance, credit, liquidity, settlement, custody, operational and access risks.13 They apply to designated systemically important arrangements through the relevant legal and supervisory framework. A network's technical decentralisation does not answer whether it performs an FMI function.

CPMI-IOSCO guidance confirms that a systemically important stablecoin arrangement should observe relevant PFMIs.14 The arrangement includes governance, transfer, settlement and reserve functions, not only the issuer. For Pakistan, designation and oversight must rest on statute and transparent criteria.

IOSCO's 2023 recommendations address regulatory outcomes for trading, custody, conflicts, disclosure, market abuse, retail distribution and cross-border cooperation.15 They are designed for consistent outcomes while allowing domestic legal forms. They do not decide whether a particular token is a security under Pakistani law.

IOSCO's DeFi recommendations focus on responsible persons and economically equivalent functions.16 Multi-function platforms create conflicts where listing, trading, proprietary dealing, custody and lending are combined. Pakistan can respond through separation, disclosure, governance and capital, but must identify who is legally responsible and why.

The IMF-FSB Synthesis Paper and IMF policy elements examine macro-financial stability, monetary sovereignty, capital-flow management, tax and institutional capacity.17 Their analytical value is greatest where digital assets interact with external accounts and domestic payment confidence. They are not domestic prohibitions or licences.

Technical assistance can strengthen legislation, data and supervision. Programme conditionality, where agreed under an IMF arrangement, has a different source and effect from a general staff paper. World Bank development work adds inclusion, infrastructure and institutional perspectives. Pakistan should disclose which proposition comes from which instrument.

The OECD Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework identifies reporting cryptoasset service providers, relevant cryptoassets, reportable users and transactions for exchange of tax information.18 Its tax-transparency taxonomy is purpose-specific. It should not silently determine PVARA licensing or private-law ownership.

Implementation requires domestic legislation, competent-authority arrangements, due diligence, data safeguards and information-exchange infrastructure. A reporting obligation should specify persons, fields, valuation rules, retention and remedies. International exchange must operate within applicable confidentiality and taxpayer protections.

Pakistan’s CARF question is: what legal and technical chain would allow FBR to receive and, where lawfully arranged, exchange reliable tax information on crypto-asset transactions? The OECD’s CARF is an international tax-transparency framework. Its three components are model rules and commentary for domestic transposition, a multilateral competent authority agreement or other exchange arrangements, and an XML schema for reporting and exchange. Its four substantive building blocks concern relevant crypto-assets, reporting service providers, reportable transactions and information, and due diligence to identify users, controlling persons and tax residence.19

Pakistan’s baseline is section 66 of the VAA, the Income Tax Ordinance and FBR’s existing tax-administration powers analysed in Chapter 23. A VASP licence can identify a regulated population and produce data, but it does not by itself create a CARF reporting nexus, define reportable users and controlling persons, require tax-residence self-certification, identify reportable transaction classes, establish valuation and aggregation, authorise international exchange, or satisfy confidentiality and data-safeguard requirements. Those are tax-law and administrative-cooperation questions. PVARA may supply a verified licensee list and lawfully held data; FBR must own the tax-reporting rule and competent-authority chain.

Pakistan’s implementation-status question is: has an international CARF commitment already supplied the missing legal basis? On the OECD commitments list last updated 23 June 2026, Pakistan is not shown among jurisdictions committed to commence CARF exchanges in 2027, 2028 or 2029; it is also absent from the CARF-MCAA signatories list stated to be current as of 3 March 2026. Absence from those lists does not prohibit Pakistan from adopting domestic reporting or later committing. It means this chapter must not state that Pakistan has made a CARF exchange commitment or that the CARF-MCAA presently authorises exchange for Pakistan.20

Pakistan’s DAC8 question is: what can a binding EU implementation model reveal about the domestic machinery CARF requires? DAC8 amends the EU administrative-cooperation regime. It requires reporting and due diligence by reporting crypto-asset service providers, information on reportable users and controlling persons, annual reporting, records, compliance procedures and exchange between tax administrations. It also reaches defined crypto-asset operators outside MiCA’s authorisation population through a registration architecture. Its first reporting period begins from 1 January 2026. DAC8 expressly operates as tax administration; MiCA authorisation data feeds it but does not replace it.21

The transferable lesson is a separate tax-information lane connected to, but not absorbed by, PVARA licensing. Pakistan would need primary authority or valid tax rules for nexus, due diligence, fields, reportable transactions, valuation, corrections, retention, inspection and sanctions; a PVARA–FBR data gateway with purpose and access controls; secure schema testing; and an international legal basis before exchange. The non-transferable features are EU member-state allocation, single registration and automatic exchange under Union law. The chapter therefore sequences feasibility, domestic legislation, safeguards, technical readiness and any commitment decision. Chapter 23 does not recommend declaring CARF operational by press release.

The 2023 UNIDROIT Principles address digital assets, control, custody, innocent acquisition, secured transactions, enforcement and insolvency.22 They offer a coherent vocabulary for private-law reform and technology-neutral connecting rules. They are principles, not a self-executing global property code.

Pakistani courts and drafters may use the Principles as persuasive comparative material where consistent with domestic law. Binding rules on priority, insolvency or third-party effects require valid enactment or judicial development within authorised doctrine. Citation should never be represented as incorporation.

The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in 2019 that holdings of cryptocurrencies generally fall within IAS 2 when held for sale in the ordinary course of business and otherwise within IAS 38, on the facts described.23 That agenda decision addresses accounting, not legal ownership or regulatory status. New contractual token rights may require separate analysis.

Comparable accounts require valuation policies, control evidence, liability recognition and disclosures about concentration and custody. Prudential supervisors may impose treatment beyond accounting measurement. Audit evidence must address keys, rights and obligations, not merely inspect a public balance.

Supervisory colleges and memoranda can coordinate group risk, licensing changes, cyber incidents and failure planning. They do not merge regulators or transfer coercive power by implication. The home and host authority, legal gateways and decision rights must remain clear.

Information exchange should have a defined purpose, security classification, retention rule and correction process. Adverse action should rest on disclosable reasons or lawful protected procedures. Confidential cooperation cannot become an unreviewable blacklist.

Standards can evidence recognised risk, inform proportionality and shape external market access. Pakistan’s Virtual Assets Act 2026 and PVARA regulations notified on 21 August 2026 refer to international standards within their respective statutory and delegated scope. Regulators should publish a concordance showing the exact domestic instrument and any national adaptation.

The operative publication question is which Pakistani instrument gives a particular international proposition legal effect. A domestic concordance should record the originating body and version, outcome sought, adopt/adapt/reject decision, competent institution, enabling provision, instrument, commencement, affected persons, safeguards, implementation evidence and review date. This prevents an examination practice, reporting form or software field from silently extending the approved rule.

Standards interact but use different taxonomies. A VASP under FATF, a cryptoasset service provider under MiCA, a reporting provider under CARF and a prudential exposure under Basel are not necessarily coextensive. Verified data may be reused where lawful, but the purpose and boundary of each category must remain visible. A universal provider flag can produce both over-reporting and gaps.

Supervisory colleges should exchange facts before conclusions. They may share group structure, custody chain, incidents and risk controls under lawful gateways. Each regulator then applies its own statute and gives reasons. Where confidential foreign information cannot be disclosed to the affected firm, domestic procedure should still provide the substance necessary for a meaningful answer unless a lawful exception applies.

Standards require revision control. FATF Recommendations, Basel treatment and technical reporting formats change. Domestic incorporation should specify whether later versions apply automatically; open-ended ambulatory incorporation may raise delegation and notice concerns. For coercive rules, the safer method is a reasoned domestic amendment with a stated effective date, transition and historical archive.

Implementation evidence should be matched to purpose. FATF effectiveness cannot be proved by counting registrations alone; Basel compliance cannot be proved by a policy if exposure data are unreliable; IOSCO outcomes cannot be proved by the number of warnings; CARF readiness cannot be proved by a data schema without lawful reporting and exchange. Pakistan’s reports should distinguish instrument issued, capability tested, live outcome and unresolved limitation.

Named officers in PVARA, SBP, SECP, FMU and FBR should own standards relevant to their mandates; a coordination process should maintain the concordance and identify overlaps; and each body should make and defend its own instrument. Parliamentary and public reporting should identify the recommendation, domestic rule, responsible institution, implementation evidence, limitation and planned revision. Pakistan may adopt an outcome through a different instrument, defer it for capacity reasons or reject a technique that conflicts with domestic law, provided the disposition is reasoned, public and lawful.
Transnational standards coordinate; they do not replace domestic law. Pakistan should implement selected outcomes lawfully and recheck every later use.

This chapter applies public international law to cross-border digital-asset activity. It distinguishes prescriptive, adjudicative and enforcement jurisdiction; examines nationality, attribution, treaties, sanctions, cyber operations, mutual legal assistance, confiscation, investment protection and CBDCs; and sets limits on unilateral extraterritorial regulation. Its central claim is that international standards and technical reach must not be confused with a lawful jurisdictional basis.

Digital-asset systems engage monetary stability, taxation, crime, sanctions, trade, investment, privacy and cyber resilience. Most actors and assets remain private, but states regulate persons, firms, infrastructure and effects within recognised jurisdiction. A protocol is not ordinarily an international legal person merely because it operates across borders.1

There is no single international-law category called “digital asset” with uniform incidents. A CBDC, stablecoin claim, tokenised share and unbacked protocol asset present different issuers, obligations and state interests. Legal analysis should begin with conduct, person, right and connecting fact.

Territorial jurisdiction can attach to conduct, persons, establishments, servers, intermediaries or substantial effects, depending on the rule invoked. Network distribution may multiply connections but does not make all states equally competent. Enforcement on foreign territory ordinarily requires consent or another international-law basis.2

States retain authority to define legal tender, regulate payment systems, supervise financial institutions and protect monetary stability within international obligations. Private denomination does not extinguish that authority. Measures must nevertheless comply with treaty commitments, human rights and general principles applicable to the state.

Stablecoins make the jurisdictional chain especially visible. An issuer, reserve custodian, payment interface and customer may be in four states. A domestic rule can protect local customers and impose conditions on service into Pakistan, but reserve enforcement abroad depends on the governing claim, local law and cooperation. A foreign issuer's use of the dollar may create US regulatory or sanctions exposure; it does not give the United States exclusive jurisdiction over every holder dispute.

Territory and nationality are primary bases; protective and passive-personality principles may operate in defined circumstances, while universal jurisdiction is exceptional and offence-specific. A state claiming jurisdiction should identify the basis and a genuine connection. Customer accessibility on a global website should not automatically create unlimited worldwide jurisdiction.3

Concurrent prescriptions can expose a platform to inconsistent duties. Comity, consultation and reasonableness can reduce conflict, but they do not erase mandatory law. Domestic orders to produce overseas records must observe the applicable statute, blocking rules, treaties and the territorial limits of coercion.4

Application begins by disaggregating a cross-border event. Consider a foreign exchange used by Pakistani customers that suffers a cyber theft and later freezes withdrawals. Pakistan may have a territorial or effects connection to local marketing and loss, nationality jurisdiction over Pakistani actors, regulatory jurisdiction over service into the market, and a basis to request evidence abroad. Those connections do not authorise Pakistani investigators to seize a foreign server or compel a foreign bank inside another state without consent, treaty process or the requested state's law. Figure 24.1 later sets out the corresponding jurisdiction-and-cooperation sequence.

A state may regulate its nationals abroad within international-law limits. Corporate nationality ordinarily follows legal criteria such as incorporation or seat, while beneficial ownership is relevant to control, sanctions and financial integrity but does not itself settle nationality for every purpose.5

Offshore incorporation does not remove conduct from a state's jurisdiction where nationals direct it or domestic customers, infrastructure or harm supply a statutory connection. Conversely, beneficial ownership or token possession alone should not be treated as a universal basis. The domestic statute must authorise the claimed extraterritorial reach.

State responsibility requires conduct attributable to a state and breach of an international obligation.6 Technical harm, market loss or regulatory disagreement is not enough. The content and temporal application of the primary obligation must be established before remedies are considered.

Conduct of state organs is attributable to the state; private conduct may be attributable in circumstances addressed by Articles 5, 8 or 11 of the ILC Articles. Funding, location or political sympathy is not necessarily direction or control. Attribution of a cyber-enabled asset theft therefore requires evidence about both the operation and the state's relationship to it.7

Cyber attribution requires two distinct proofs. Technical attribution links infrastructure, malware, wallets or operators to conduct. Legal attribution links that conduct to a state under the applicable rule. Confidence in one does not automatically establish the other. Public statements, countermeasures and criminal charges should communicate the evidential and legal basis appropriate to their consequence. Where facts remain uncertain, cooperation and protective action may be lawful even though a final state-responsibility claim is premature.

Relevant instruments may include investment treaties, trade commitments, tax agreements, sanctions obligations, UN conventions against corruption and transnational organised crime, and cybercrime cooperation instruments.8 Each has its own parties, scope, reservations and implementation. FATF standards are not treaties.9

International organisations possess only conferred competence. A recommendation by one body cannot expand another's treaty mandate or directly amend Pakistani law. Domestic implementation must follow Pakistan's constitutional allocation and applicable legislation.10

International organisations can assist with typologies, training and coordination, but no organisation should be cited beyond its competence. FATF addresses financial-integrity standards, the FSB financial stability, and UN bodies their respective Charter or treaty mandates. Pakistan's submissions and legislation should preserve those differences. Institutional clarity strengthens the credibility of both cooperation requests and domestic action.

Pakistan signed UNCAC on 9 December 2003, ratified it on 31 August 2007, and became bound on 30 September 2007. Its current depositary record contains an Article 66(3) reservation to compulsory arbitration and ICJ referral, states that UNCAC is not its legal basis for extradition, and designates NAB as the Article 46(13) central authority for English-language requests.11 Pakistan signed UNTOC on 14 December 2000, ratified it on 13 January 2010, and became bound on 12 February 2010. Its Article 35(3) reservation excludes Article 35(2); its declarations state that UNTOC is not its legal basis for extradition and designate the Ministry of Interior as the Article 18(13) central authority for English-language requests.12

Pakistan is not listed as a party, signatory or invited State in the current official records for the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime. It is also absent from the current Netherlands depositary list for the 2019 HCCH Judgments Convention.13 Those instruments may remain useful models or future cooperation routes, but their provisions must not be presented as present treaty obligations of Pakistan. Signature, ratification, entry into force, reservation, institutional designation and domestic implementation are separate status fields.

The same discipline applies to international-organisational material. A resolution, recommendation, assessment and binding Security Council decision have different effects. Pakistan should label each instrument in official registers and court submissions and identify the domestic implementing measure where one is required. Accurate status is an operational safeguard because it prevents cooperation from becoming an unsupported exercise of coercive power.

UN Security Council measures adopted under the Charter and unilateral national sanctions have different sources and reach.14 Countermeasures under the law of state responsibility are also distinct: they respond to a prior internationally wrongful act and are constrained by purpose, proportionality and protected obligations.15

Digital assets can be blocked, moved through intermediaries or used in evasion. Effective controls require address and person attribution, provider obligations and review. A blockchain analytics flag is evidence, not a final legal designation; freezing and forfeiture require the relevant authority and protections for affected third parties.16

Sanctions analysis should similarly separate designation, blocking and confiscation. A valid designation may require a regulated firm to freeze an asset and prohibit dealing. Title may remain with the designated person unless the governing law provides forfeiture. A later return, confiscation or transfer requires additional authority. A service provider should preserve the legal basis, match evidence, human decision and review record rather than make permanent deprivation depend on an address-screening score.

Attacks on exchanges, bridges, payment systems or central-bank infrastructure may trigger domestic crime, state responsibility or, at high thresholds, Charter questions. Not every cyber incident constitutes a use of force or armed attack. The legal character depends on scale, effects, attribution and the rule invoked.17

States should maintain incident response, preserve evidence and cooperate through lawful channels. Claims of a general duty to prevent every harmful transnational transaction remain contested; specific treaty, sanctions, AML and cybercrime duties provide firmer grounds. Response measures must remain necessary and proportionate.

Investigators often need subscriber records, device evidence, exchange logs and testimony across borders. Mutual legal assistance, police cooperation, direct provider channels where lawful and joint investigations can assist. None supplies automatic coercive power inside another state.18

Digital value may move before a formal request is processed. Preservation mechanisms and emergency contacts can reduce delay, but production, admissibility and extradition remain treaty- and statute-dependent. Dual criminality concerns conduct, not identical offence names.19

The same cross-border event may generate private claims and public cooperation. Customers may sue under contract or property law; PVARA may act against a local entity or permission; FIA or another competent agency may investigate an offence; FMU channels may support financial intelligence; and a foreign insolvency representative may seek recognition. Public international law governs state-to-state authority and cooperation, while private international law allocates forum and governing law. Treating one as a substitute for the other produces overreach or remedial gaps.

For Pakistan, a practical international-readiness package would identify treaty and non-treaty channels, official contacts, preservation procedures, standards for incoming and outgoing requests, confidentiality, third-party rights and review. It would separately state the domestic nexus for foreign providers and the limits of administrative orders. Sections 4 and 17 of the Virtual Assets Act, 2026 expressly contemplate foreign-regulator and law-enforcement cooperation, while the Mutual Legal Assistance (Criminal Matters) Act, 2020 supplies the general statutory request machinery.20 This package would improve enforcement more than a broad declaration that all transactions involving a Pakistani are subject to Pakistani law.

Routing must be instrument-specific. The UNCAC depositary notice still designates NAB for Article 46 requests, whereas UNTOC designates the Ministry of Interior and the 2020 Act, as amended in 2021, defines the Secretary, Ministry of Interior, as the general statutory central authority.21 The chapter therefore records the difference and requires coordination rather than silently replacing one designation with another.

Public reporting can strengthen reciprocity. Competent bodies should publish aggregate data on assistance requests, preservation, restraints, returns and time to execute, while protecting investigations and personal information. Reasons for recurrent refusal—insufficient nexus, dual criminality, data-law conflict or defective process—can guide treaty and legislative improvement. Cooperation should be evaluated by lawful results, not request volume.
Figure 24.1 sets out the sequence from connecting facts to a lawful domestic act, foreign request or narrowed response.

Confiscation requires a legal basis, jurisdiction over the person or property and proof under the applicable regime. UNCAC Chapter V provides a framework for international asset recovery in corruption matters; UNTOC Articles 12–14 address confiscation and international cooperation in its field.22 Private keys may make control practical; they do not establish legal title or forfeiture.

Victims, customers, secured creditors and innocent purchasers may claim the same pool. A requested state may apply its own procedure and public policy. Orders should describe the asset or value, preserve notice and challenge, and distinguish temporary freezing from final confiscation and return.23

Asset recovery should be integrated into a cooperation package from the beginning. A request must distinguish information, temporary preservation, freezing, confiscation and return; identify the asset or value; and disclose the relevant proceeding and third-party claims. Wallet control may allow rapid technical movement, so competent authorities need secure custody procedures. Yet speed cannot erase the requirement to document legal custody, evidential continuity and the final basis for disposition.

A digital-asset enterprise or right may qualify as an “investment” only if the applicable treaty and jurisdictional requirements are satisfied. Token ownership alone does not guarantee treaty coverage. Corporate nationality, legality of the investment, territorial nexus and consent to arbitration remain decisive. The ICSID Convention entered into force for Pakistan on 15 October 1966, but Article 25 still requires written consent to the particular class or dispute.24

Licensing change, prohibition or seizure may generate treaty claims, but states retain regulatory space under treaty text and general doctrine. Legitimate expectations usually require specific legal context or representations; policy optimism is not a stabilisation guarantee. Transition, reasons and due process reduce both public-law and treaty risk.

Investment treaties add a further reason for calibrated transition. Abrupt revocation, discrimination or uncompensated taking may be alleged by a qualifying investor, while good-faith financial regulation remains a legitimate public function. Pakistan should preserve published conditions, reliance periods where justified, reasons, proportionality and review. These practices protect domestic legality whether or not a treaty ultimately applies. Pakistan's Arbitration (International Investment Disputes) Act, 2011 implements the ICSID framework domestically but does not dispense with treaty, nationality, investment and consent requirements.25

CBDCs are central-bank liabilities governed by public monetary law. Cross-border use requires decisions about access, foreign-exchange control, settlement, data and monetary spillovers. A technical bridge cannot allocate these sovereign responsibilities.

CBDC cooperation should be developed through explicit institutional arrangements. Cross-border settlement raises access to central-bank liabilities, foreign-exchange management, operating hours, cyber responsibility, data localisation, failure and dispute questions. A common technical platform cannot decide monetary allocation. Each central bank and participating state must approve the relevant legal and operational terms.

CBDC and supervisory systems may affect privacy, expression, equality, property interests and access to essential services. The ICCPR protects privacy, expression and equality, though it contains no general property clause. Pakistan signed the Covenant on 17 April 2008, ratified it on 23 June 2010 and became bound on 23 September 2010. Its surviving reservations concern Articles 3 and 25, not Articles 17, 19 or 26 used here.26 Design should minimise data, separate functions, authorise access and provide human review and remedies.

Human rights should operate throughout, not only in CBDC design. Financial surveillance and account restriction can affect privacy, expression, equality, livelihood and procedural fairness. Restrictions may be justified for crime prevention or financial stability, but must have a legal basis and be necessary and proportionate under the applicable standard. Cross-border cooperation should not be used to evade protections that would apply to domestic action.27

States can project rules through reserve currencies, app stores, banks and global platforms. Economic leverage is not a complete legal justification. Overbroad claims invite conflicting orders, data-law breaches and market fragmentation, particularly where every state treats remote accessibility as domestic operation.

A principled order identifies a substantial connection, states extraterritorial scope, coordinates with affected authorities and limits remedies to what can lawfully be enforced. Pakistan should combine local customer protection with treaties, assistance arrangements and conflict rules rather than claim control over a borderless network. Table 24.1 summarises the recurring bases, limits and cooperative routes.

The final public-international-law test is reciprocity of principle. Pakistan may object when foreign states regulate remote conduct on a thin connection; it should apply a disciplined nexus to its own claims. It may seek rapid foreign preservation; it should offer lawful channels and rights when responding. A digital-asset order that treats sovereignty, cooperation and due process consistently will be more enforceable abroad and more legitimate at home.

That discipline should survive emergency conditions. Urgency may justify preservation or interim restraint where legislation permits, but not an invented jurisdictional basis or permanent deprivation without process. Recorded authority, necessity, duration and review make rapid digital-asset action both more defensible and more likely to receive cooperation abroad.

Public international law remains fully relevant to digital assets. It disciplines the leap from technical reach to legal authority and distinguishes domestic regulation, international obligation and cooperation. The durable method is connection, competence, attribution, process and remedy—not the assertion that decentralisation makes every state powerless or universally competent.
Authorities are supplied as true page footnotes at the propositions they support.

A single transaction may involve an issuer in one state, protocol contributors in several, a custodian and sub-custodian elsewhere, a user in Pakistan and validator infrastructure worldwide. These facts create potential connections, not an answer. The relevant relationship may be contractual, proprietary, regulatory, tortious or insolvency-related.

A ledger copy exists in many places and a private key can move without changing the underlying claim. Server, node, key, owner and exchange locations can point in different directions. Any situs rule should be selected for a legal purpose and protect ascertainable third-party expectations.

Jurisdiction may rest on presence, residence, submission, contractual forum, conduct or legally relevant harm, subject to domestic procedure. For unknown defendants, evidence may initially identify only addresses and transactions. Courts should require a real connection and useful relief rather than infer jurisdiction from worldwide accessibility.

Platform terms often select a foreign forum. Courts should examine incorporation, notice, bargaining context, consumer protections and overriding statutes before enforcing the clause. Anti-suit, stay and parallel-proceeding rules must preserve comity and access to justice; boilerplate should not defeat mandatory protection by design.

An express choice can govern contractual obligations if valid and sufficiently identified. It cannot necessarily determine proprietary effects against strangers. Without a choice, courts use the objectively closest or most real connection under the forum's method, considering performance, residence, intermediary and transaction structure.

Licensing, sanctions, consumer, AML, insolvency and market-integrity rules may apply irrespective of contractual choice. Public policy is an exceptional control, not a licence to disregard foreign law whenever outcomes differ. Courts should state which mandatory interest overrides and why.

Proposed connecting factors include the owner's residence, location of the key, issuer, system, relevant intermediary or chosen law. Each works better for some assets than others. Owner residence may be unstable; key location may be secret or replicated; a permissionless network may have no issuer or administration.

Legislation should use a hierarchy. For an intermediated holding, the law expressly governing the account or custody relationship can determine proprietary effects if third parties can ascertain it and protected persons are not prejudiced. For an issuer-based asset, issuer or system law may be appropriate. Control is a factual and legal concept, not a geographic point.

A platform customer's claim may be a proprietary interest in identified assets, a beneficial interest in a pool, or a personal claim for delivery. The distinction governs priority, tracing and insolvency. Courts in Ruscoe v Cryptopia and ByBit Fintech Ltd v Ho Kai Xin recognised property and trust consequences on their particular laws and facts.1

The law governing proprietary effects should determine whether transfer occurs, whether a good-faith acquirer is protected and how security interests rank. The law governing a contract determines promises and damages. Remedies may be governed by the forum while depending on foreign-law rights; the categories should not be collapsed.

Issuer terms can choose law for issuer obligations and define redemption. Protocol rules describe technical validity but may not constitute an agreed choice among all holders. A governance vote can alter software; it cannot automatically amend a contract or extinguish property rights governed by law.

Forks can create competing records, assets or communities. The legal consequence depends on exchange terms, custody duties, issuer promises and applicable property law. Where no central counterparty exists, courts should identify persons who made representations or exercised control rather than attribute obligations to a network label.

Omnibus accounts, individually segregated addresses, hosted wallets and non-custodial software allocate control differently. Contract, trust and regulatory status must be read together. A hosted-wallet balance can be an internal ledger claim even if the provider controls pooled on-chain assets.

Cross-border sub-custody raises governing-law and insolvency questions at each tier. The primary custodian should disclose location and law, obtain records, reconcile holdings and preserve return rights. Contractual segregation that is not effective under the sub-custodian's insolvency law can provide false comfort.

Consumer rules may protect residents despite foreign terms where a business directs activity toward them. Investor-protection rules may apply to domestic offers or market conduct. The test should examine language, currency, marketing, customer acceptance and service design rather than mere website availability.

An interface operator may select assets, route orders, charge fees or block users even where settlement occurs through a protocol. Those functions may create contractual, tortious or regulatory responsibility. Software publication alone presents different facts. “Decentralised” is a conclusion to prove, not a conflicts rule.

In Pakistan, sections 13 and 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 govern the conclusiveness and presumption concerning foreign judgments, subject to statutory exceptions including want of jurisdiction, absence of merits, natural justice, fraud and breach of Pakistani law.2 Reciprocity and execution procedure must be distinguished from recognition at common law.

English cases have authorised service and information relief against persons unknown and exchanges where procedural requirements were met.3 Recognition abroad depends on the requested state's rules and the nature of the order. A worldwide freezing label does not make the order self-executing in every country.

Cross-border insolvency requires identification of the debtor, proceeding and applicable recognition mechanism. The UNCITRAL Model Law offers a centre-of-main-interests architecture, but it operates only where enacted.4 Pakistan should not be described as having adopted it without current statutory confirmation.

Recognition of a foreign proceeding does not determine whether customer assets belong to the debtor. Governing property and trust law, records and tracing remain relevant. Courts and office-holders need protocols for data, realisation and distribution while protecting local claimants and due process.

Interim orders can prevent dissipation and identify defendants, but require urgency, evidence, undertakings and fair return dates. LMN v Bitflyer Holdings Inc illustrates disclosure against exchanges to trace cryptoassets.5 The order's effectiveness depended on identifiable intermediaries and cooperation.

Failure can involve insolvency, exploit, fraud, governance breakdown or loss of keys. Each activates different law. Supervisors and courts should preserve records and customer assets before attempting a technological cure. Recovery claims should distinguish an asset, substitute proceeds and a personal claim.

Arbitration requires an agreement binding the parties, a seat and an arbitrable dispute. Code interaction is not necessarily consent. DAO governance terms may form an agreement for some participants if validly incorporated and accepted, but cannot bind strangers merely because they used a public network.

Pakistan's Recognition and Enforcement (Arbitration Agreements and Foreign Arbitral Awards) Act 2011 implements the New York Convention framework.6 Courts may refuse enforcement only on the statutory grounds. An award directing a token transfer still requires identifiable control and must comply with sanctions and mandatory law.

Pakistan should enact purpose-specific rules: recognise express issuer or system law for issuer obligations; use an ascertainable account agreement or intermediary branch for intermediated proprietary effects; protect consumers and innocent third parties through mandatory rules; and provide fallbacks based on the closest connection. Courts should characterise the issue before selecting the law.

The regime should support evidence preservation, court-to-court and office-holder cooperation, service and recognition consistent with due process. Provider licences should require disclosure of custody locations and governing laws. Treaty accession or model-law adoption should follow constitutional and legislative process, not be assumed from policy alignment.

A Pakistani connecting statute should begin with characterisation. The court should ask whether the disputed issue concerns an issuer's obligation, a contract between customer and provider, proprietary effects of a transfer, an intermediated entitlement, security priority, insolvency, tort or remedy. The answer determines which connecting rule is relevant. Calling the subject a digital asset before identifying the issue does not advance the analysis.

For issuer-linked assets, the law validly selected in public and accessible issuer terms can govern the issuer's obligations and internal system questions, subject to mandatory rules. If the token records a share or debt, company and securities law may supply non-derogable connections. A later unilateral change to website terms should not alter accrued proprietary or contractual rights without the consent and notice required by the governing law.

For intermediated holdings, the law expressly governing the account or relevant branch can provide predictable proprietary effects where it is ascertainable and not chosen after the dispute. The licence should require the provider to disclose that law and every material sub-custody location. Consumer and innocent-third-party rules should prevent a secret choice from defeating protected expectations. Where no valid choice exists, the law of the intermediary branch maintaining the account may offer a more stable connection than key location.

For a permissionless native asset without issuer or intermediary, no connecting factor is perfect. The holder's habitual residence may be relevant to succession or insolvency but can change; the key may be distributed; network governance may be diffuse. A statutory fallback should select the closest connection for the precise issue and permit consideration of control, parties, transaction and protected third-party expectations. Courts should avoid transforming a pragmatic interim situs into a universal rule.

Remedies require a second-stage analysis. A Pakistani court may have personal jurisdiction over a defendant and issue an order concerning assets, but compliance by a foreign exchange or recognition abroad depends on foreign procedure. Information and freezing orders should be targeted to identified providers and supported by evidence. Service on persons unknown can preserve a claim, yet eventual liability still requires identity, notice and proof.

Cross-border insolvency is where poor connecting rules become distributive loss. A foreign court may recognise the main proceeding and cooperate with a liquidator, yet still need to determine whether wallet assets are held on trust, pooled for customers or owned by the debtor. Records must connect on-chain control to legal liabilities. Provider regulation should require a failure data pack containing customer entitlements, addresses, keys or control process, sub-custodians, governing terms, liens and reconciliation history.

Arbitration can improve specialist dispute resolution for commercial counterparties, but it cannot solve every digital-asset dispute. An unknown fraudster did not consent; customers may be protected against unfair clauses; proprietary priority may affect non-parties; insolvency and regulatory matters may be non-arbitrable or reserved. Smart-contract execution should be treated as evidence of performance, not automatic proof of agreement or legal correctness.

Recognition policy should be reciprocal and rights-conscious. Sections 13 and 14 CPC supply core Pakistani controls for foreign judgments. Reform could clarify digital service, interim orders and cooperation, but should preserve want of jurisdiction, natural justice, fraud and public-policy protections. Accession to a judgments convention or enactment of the Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency would require a separate legislative decision and implementation plan.

Provider licensing can reduce litigation uncertainty before a case arises. Terms should name the contracting entity, governing law and forum; explain whether the customer owns assets or has a delivery claim; identify custody and sub-custody; state fork and airdrop treatment; and preserve complaint and insolvency contacts. PVARA should review these disclosures without purporting to decide foreign property law conclusively.

The proposed statutory approach is therefore modest but powerful: characterise first, recognise transparent choices for the relationship they can legitimately govern, protect third parties and consumers, provide stable fallbacks, and coordinate judgments and insolvency through lawful procedure. It does not require Pakistan to declare where every digital asset is located. It requires courts and market participants to know which law answers each question.

Judicial education and evidence rules will determine whether the method works. Courts need intelligible proof of foreign law, wallet control, exchange records, protocol events and custody architecture. Experts may explain technical facts or foreign law according to procedure; they should not decide the ultimate legal issue. Orders should use technology-neutral descriptions and permit identification by address, transaction hash and equivalent evidence without assuming those identifiers prove ownership.

PVARA, courts and insolvency institutions should also preserve a standard failure record. A licensed provider's contracts, customer ledger, on-chain addresses, sub-custody confirmations, governance keys, incident history and legal opinions should be exportable in durable form. That record would not predetermine title, but it would make a cross-border determination possible before records and personnel disperse.

These institutional measures complete the conflicts rules. Predictable governing law, targeted interim relief, recognition and cooperation all depend on reliable facts and usable records.
